title: Genes
objective: After this level you can explain what a gene does and how genes lead to proteins.
summary: A gene is a stretch of DNA; about 20,000 of yours code for proteins. A cell copies a gene into messenger RNA, and a ribosome reads it to build a protein.

cards.headline: The recipes are kept in the nucleus. The kitchen is outside.
cards.body: Most of your DNA sits in the nucleus, but the machines that build proteins, called ribosomes, work out in the cytoplasm. So how does a recipe reach the kitchen? Follow one gene.

cards.headline: A gene is one recipe
cards.body: A gene is a stretch of DNA, the basic unit of heredity. Many genes are instructions for making a protein; many others act like switches that control other genes. You have about 20,000 protein-coding genes, and together they fill less than 2 percent of your DNA. If your DNA is a cookbook, a gene is one recipe.

cards.headline: Proteins do the work
cards.body: The dish is a protein, and proteins do most of the work in your cells. Some are enzymes that run chemical reactions, some carry messages between cells, and some give cells their structure. Each is a chain built from 20 kinds of amino acids, strung like pearls on a necklace. The order of the pearls sets the protein's shape, and the shape sets its job.

cards.headline: From recipe to dish in two steps
cards.body: First, transcription: the cell copies a gene into messenger RNA, a working copy that carries the message out of the nucleus. Then translation: a ribosome in the cytoplasm reads that copy three letters at a time. Each three-letter codon usually calls for one amino acid, and the ribosome links them in order. The original recipe stays safely on the shelf.

mascot.line: Keep the order: copy the recipe first, then build from the copy.

cards.fact: A gene makes a protein, not a person.
cards.context: Most traits don't come down to one gene. Height, for example, is shaped by hundreds of gene variants, each with a small effect, plus things like nutrition. Genes supply the recipes; a whole body is more like a banquet.

cards.headline: Genes: decoded
learned: A gene is a stretch of DNA, often a protein recipe
Transcription into messenger RNA, translation by a ribosome
Most traits involve many genes plus environment

questions.prompt: About how many protein-coding genes do humans have?

options.label: About 2 million
options.rationale: Far too many for the human genome.

questions.explanation: NHGRI puts the human count at about 20,000 protein-coding genes.

questions.prompt: Why does a cell copy a gene into messenger RNA before building a protein?

options.label: The RNA is the cell's fuel
The copy carries the message out of the nucleus to a ribosome
It turns the gene into a new chromosome
options.rationale: Chromosomes stay as they are; the copy is temporary.

options.label: It destroys genes the cell no longer needs
options.rationale: The original gene stays in place.

questions.explanation: Messenger RNA carries the gene's message out of the nucleus to the ribosomes in the cytoplasm, which build the protein.

questions.prompt: Level 5 said the order of DNA's letters carries meaning. How does a ribosome read a gene's message?

options.label: One letter at a time, each letter one protein
options.rationale: Proteins are built from many amino acids.

options.label: Two letters at a time, each pair one gene
options.rationale: Genes are long stretches of DNA.

options.label: All 3 billion letters at once
options.rationale: It reads one short messenger copy.

options.label: Three letters at a time, each codon one amino acid

questions.explanation: A ribosome reads messenger RNA in three-letter codons, and each codon usually calls for one amino acid.
